claim: Haiti reported a total of 8828 malaria cases (presumed and confirmed) in 2019.
source: Malaria transmission in Haiti is endemic and poses a significant public health problem with a total of 8828 cases (presumed and confirmed) reported in 2019 (World Health Organization, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization 2019 report.

claim: Blood stage prevalence of Plasmodium falciparum is below 1% in many areas of Haiti.
source: blood stage prevalence of Plasmodium falciparum (Pf) is in many areas below 1% (Lucchi et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lucchi et al., 2014.

claim: Anopheles albimanus is the dominant local malaria vector in Haiti.
source: the dominant local vector (Anopheles albimanus) is inefficient (being primarily zoophilic and exophagic [Frederick et al., 2016])
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Frederick et al., 2016.

claim: Anopheles albimanus is primarily zoophilic and exophagic.
source: the dominant local vector (Anopheles albimanus) is inefficient (being primarily zoophilic and exophagic [Frederick et al., 2016])
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Frederick et al., 2016.

claim: Malaria elimination is a national priority in Haiti.
source: Malaria elimination is a national priority and an ambition of the National Malaria Control Program of Haiti (or PNCM; abbreviated from its official name in French: Programme National de Contrôle de la Malaria).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Haiti's national policy.

claim: The PNCM has built a working strategy around improvements to the surveillance and management system operating nationally through the health facility and community health worker network.
source: To this end, the PNCM has built a working strategy around improvements to the surveillance and management system operating nationally through the health facility and community health worker (CHW) network, and the delivery of information and interventions targeted at sub-national administrative regions hosting identified transmission foci (Boncy et al., 2015; Druetz et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boncy et al., 2015 and Druetz et al., 2018.

claim: The PNCM has collaborated with the Malaria Atlas Project and partners to geo-locate transmission foci and develop evidence-based risk stratification.
source: To precisely geo-locate transmission foci and develop an evidence-based risk stratification, the PNCM has collaborated with the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) and partners.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the collaboration.

claim: The study constructed a national-level endemicity map and seasonality profile informed by routine case reports from health facilities.
source: In this study, we describe an important component of this collaboration: the construction of a national-level endemicity map and seasonality profile informed by routine case reports from health facilities.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's objective and output.

claim: Recent years have seen great progress in the adoption of Bayesian methods for probabilistic map-making among the infectious disease and global health research community.
source: Recent years have seen great progress in the adoption of Bayesian methods for probabilistic map-making (known as model-based geostatistics; Diggle et al., 1998) among the infectious disease and global health research community (Bhatt et al., 2015; Osgood-Zimmerman et al., 2018; Zouré et al., 2014; Karagiannis-Voules et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: Model-based geostatistics is an extension to the generalised linear model whereby geographic covariates are combined with a Gaussian process representing spatially correlated residuals.
source: The standard form of this technique is an extension to the generalised linear model whereby geographic covariates based on high-resolution satellite imaging (e.g., land surface temperature; digital elevation; nighttime lights) are combined additively with a Gaussian process representing spatially correlated residuals.
evidence: This is a description of the standard methodology.

claim: Routine case reporting data in sub-Saharan Africa have historically been highly incomplete and/or subject to problematic sources of bias.
source: In the case of malaria, these methods provide benchmark estimates of transmission intensity (World Health Organization, 2019; Weiss et al., 2019; Battle et al., 2019) for much of sub-Saharan Africa where (1) routine case reporting data have historically been highly incomplete and/or subject to problematic sources of bias (Rowe et al., 2009; Alegana et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rowe et al., 2009 and Alegana et al., 2020.

claim: In low transmission settings such as Haiti, transmission typically becomes increasingly focalised.
source: In low transmission settings such as Haiti, transmission typically becomes increasingly focalised, and the low prevalence of patent parasitaemia forces community parasite surveys towards very intensive (viz. expensive) sampling designs to achieve confident spatial stratifications.
evidence: This is a general statement about low transmission settings applied to Haiti.

claim: Low prevalence of patent parasitaemia forces community parasite surveys towards very intensive sampling designs to achieve confident spatial stratifications.
source: In low transmission settings such as Haiti, transmission typically becomes increasingly focalised, and the low prevalence of patent parasitaemia forces community parasite surveys towards very intensive (viz. expensive) sampling designs to achieve confident spatial stratifications.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for survey design in low prevalence settings.

claim: Spatio-temporal risk modelling from routine passive surveillance data may be a more effective means of describing malaria heterogeneity in low transmission settings than community parasite surveys.
source: Spatio-temporal risk modelling from data deriving from a routine passive surveillance process, such as the reporting of health facility case counts, may thus be a more effective means of describing the heterogeneity of malaria in this setting.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential effectiveness of the approach.

claim: A major challenge in disease mapping from health facility case data is that case counts represent aggregation over an area of unknown extent (the health facility catchment).
source: Foremost of these is that the case count from a given facility represents the aggregation of observable case incidence over all households over an area of unknown extent: the health facility catchment.
evidence: This is a statement about a known methodological challenge.

claim: Extension of the MGB framework requires development of a sophisticated sub-model linking fine-scale disease process with aggregate data.
source: Extension of the MGB framework requires the development of a sophisticated sub-model linking the fine-scale disease process with the aggregate data (Wilson and Wakefield, 2020; Taylor et al., 2018; Sturrock et al., 2014), including a representation of health facility choice and attendance (Duncan et al., 2016; Nelli et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant methodological literature.

claim: There is a lack of information regarding spatio-temporal variations in treatment seeking propensities across Haitian communities.
source: Further challenges include a lack of information regarding spatio-temporal variations in treatment seeking propensities across the studied communities (Alegana et al., 2017b; Alegana et al., 2012; Battle et al., 2016; Karyana et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to relevant literature on treatment seeking behavior.

claim: There is a lack of information regarding spatio-temporal variations in diagnostic practices operating at each health facility in Haiti.
source: Further challenges include a lack of information regarding spatio-temporal variations in treatment seeking propensities across the studied communities (Alegana et al., 2017b; Alegana et al., 2012; Battle et al., 2016; Karyana et al., 2016) and in the diagnostic practices operating at each health facility (Bastiaens et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bastiaens et al., 2014.

claim: Validation of down-scaling models is uniquely challenging because hold-out of aggregate response data is of limited utility for testing fine-scale accuracy.
source: Validation of model outputs from this class of 'down-scaling' models is also uniquely challenging; the hold-out of aggregate response data is of limited utility for testing fine-scale accuracy, since only ancillary point-level observations can overcome the potential for 'ecological fallacy' (Wakefield and Smith, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wakefield and Smith, 2016.

claim: Serological tools that quantify immune responses to malaria antigens can reveal whether an individual has ever carried a Plasmodium falciparum parasite infection.
source: For example, serological tools that quantify immune responses to particular malaria antigens can reveal whether or not an individual has ever carried a Pf parasite infection (Corran et al., 2007; Helb et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corran et al., 2007 and Helb et al., 2015.

claim: Serological data targeting lifetime exposure history gain statistical power from lower sampling variance at the expense of temporal precision.
source: serological tools that quantify immune responses to particular malaria antigens can reveal whether or not an individual has ever carried a Pf parasite infection (Corran et al., 2007; Helb et al., 2015), effectively targeting a higher prevalence objective (i.e., lifetime exposure history instead of current infection status) to gain statistical power from lower sampling variance at the expense of temporal precision.
evidence: This is an inference about the statistical properties of serological data.

claim: Serological data have been gathered in Haiti and used to assist with malaria risk stratification.
source: Data of this nature have been gathered in Haiti and used in various ways to assist with malaria risk stratification (Oviedo et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oviedo et al., 2020.

claim: The study used a geostatistical model informed by routine case incidence reports at monthly cadence from across Haiti over a 6-year period (2014-2019).
source: Here we present the results of a bespoke analysis designed to uncover the characteristic spatial pattern of contemporary malaria endemicity in Haiti and its spatio-temporal seasonality profile using a geostatistical model informed by routine case incidence reports at monthly cadence assembled from across the country over a 6-year period (2014–2019 inclusive).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and data used.

claim: The maps produced have focused the delivery of indoor residual spraying and focal mass drug administration in the Grand'Anse Department in South-Western Haiti.
source: These maps have focussed the delivery of indoor residual spraying and focal mass drug administration in the Grand'Anse Department in South-Western Haiti.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the application of the study outputs.

claim: Large areas of Haiti, particularly in the northern departments of Nord-Ouest, Nord, and Nord-Est, and along the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range, are essentially malaria free with fewer than one in 10,000 individuals expected to experience clinical malaria each year.
source: Large areas of the country – in particular, in the northern departments of Nord-Ouest, Nord, and Nord-Est, and along the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range tracing the border of the Ouest and Sud-Est departments – are essentially malaria free with fewer than one in 10,000 individuals expected to experience clinical malarial each year.
evidence: This is a finding from the model-based analysis presented in the study.

claim: High burden malaria communities in Haiti are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments.
source: These high burden communities are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments
evidence: This is a finding from the model-based analysis presented in the study.

claim: The population-at-risk in Grand'Anse department is 322,693 (95% CI: 280,707–372,057).
source: These high burden communities are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments, with populations-at-risk (defined as those living in an area of malaria incidence greater than one case per 1000 PYO) of 322,693 (95% CI: 280,707–372,057), 322,956 (95% CI: 202,462–392,047), and 108,077 (95% CI: 61,620–147,288), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claim: The population-at-risk in Sud department is 322,956 (95% CI: 202,462–392,047).
source: These high burden communities are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments, with populations-at-risk (defined as those living in an area of malaria incidence greater than one case per 1000 PYO) of 322,693 (95% CI: 280,707–372,057), 322,956 (95% CI: 202,462–392,047), and 108,077 (95% CI: 61,620–147,288), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claim: The population-at-risk in Nippes department is 108,077 (95% CI: 61,620–147,288).
source: These high burden communities are located primarily along the coastline and rivers of the Tiburon peninsula containing the Grand'Anse, Sud, and Nippes departments, with populations-at-risk (defined as those living in an area of malaria incidence greater than one case per 1000 PYO) of 322,693 (95% CI: 280,707–372,057), 322,956 (95% CI: 202,462–392,047), and 108,077 (95% CI: 61,620–147,288), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claim: An additional area of lower but substantial malaria burden lies within the central river valley joining the Artibonite and Centre departments.
source: An additional area of lower but still substantial burden lies within the central river valley joining the Artibonite and Centre departments, with populations-at-risk of 174,766 (95% CI: 97,196–313,169) and 166,938 (95% CI: 95,070–281,816).
evidence: This is a finding from the model-based analysis.

claim: The population-at-risk in Artibonite department is 174,766 (95% CI: 97,196–313,169).
source: An additional area of lower but still substantial burden lies within the central river valley joining the Artibonite and Centre departments, with populations-at-risk of 174,766 (95% CI: 97,196–313,169) and 166,938 (95% CI: 95,070–281,816).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claim: The population-at-risk in Centre department is 166,938 (95% CI: 95,070–281,816).
source: An additional area of lower but still substantial burden lies within the central river valley joining the Artibonite and Centre departments, with populations-at-risk of 174,766 (95% CI: 97,196–313,169) and 166,938 (95% CI: 95,070–281,816).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model-based analysis.

claim: The broad credible intervals around population-at-risk estimates reflect systematic uncertainties of the de-trending, RDT-standardising, and imputation component of the model.
source: The broad credible intervals around the estimation of these populations-at-risk reflect in large part the systematic uncertainties of the de-trending, RDT-standardising, and imputation component of our model, which contribute a substantial variance to inference of the absolute clinical incidence rate, but less so to its relative spatial distribution.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model uncertainty by the authors.

claim: Regions of particularly high variance in the uncertainty summary correspond to the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range and patches along the borders of the Artibonite department and in Nord and Nord-Ouest departments.
source: Inspection of the uncertainty summary in Figure 1C indicates regions of particularly high variance corresponding to (1) the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range and (2) patches along the borders of the Artibonite department and in Nord and Nord-Ouest departments.
evidence: This is a finding from inspection of Figure 1C.

claim: High variance in the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range is explained by population sparsity combined with extreme elevation.
source: The explanation for the former is simply population sparsity (i.e., sampling noise) combined with the extreme elevation (i.e., covariate slope uncertainty)
evidence: This is an interpretation provided by the authors.

claim: The Chaîne de la Selle mountain range is probably well-classified as low malaria risk because it is believed to be an unlikely habitat for Anopheles albimanus.
source: however, since this terrain is believed to be an unlikely habitat for the local Anopheles species (principally A. albimanus) (Frederick et al., 2016), it is probably well-classified as low risk.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge about vector habitat preferences, supported by citation to Frederick et al., 2016.

claim: High variance in patches along the borders of Artibonite and in Nord and Nord-Ouest departments is explained by ongoing use of microscopic diagnosis at similar frequency to RDT diagnosis at a minority of health facilities.
source: The explanation for the latter is the ongoing use of microscopic diagnosis at similar frequency to RDT diagnosis at a minority of health facilities in these areas (most used RDT diagnosis near-exclusively in 2019), which leads to a higher contribution here from uncertainty in our standardisation procedure.
evidence: This is an interpretation provided by the authors based on the data characteristics.

claim: The accuracy of microscopic diagnosis in Haiti has been characterized as inadequate.
source: The accuracy of microscopic diagnosis in Haiti has previously been characterised as inadequate (Landman et al., 2015; Weppelmann et al., 2018), hence the importance of attempting to adjust statistically for diagnostic type.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Landman et al., 2015 and Weppelmann et al., 2018.

claim: The estimation of fine-scale spatial patterns below the extent of health facility catchments is driven by the suite of ancillary environmental covariates.
source: The estimation of fine-scale spatial patterns below the extent of health facility catchments is driven within our model by the suite of ancillary environmental covariates.
evidence: This is a statement about the model structure and how it achieves fine-scale predictions.

claim: The most important covariates for annual malaria incidence rate are elevation, accessibility, road presence/absence, and potential evapotranspiration.
source: It is interesting to note that of the four most important covariates over the entire country, three are 'topological' in nature – elevation, accessibility, and road presence/absence – and only one is climatic (potential evapotranspiration).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: The covariate importance results should not be interpreted as indicative of importance in a causal sense.
source: However, it is essential not to interpret these results as indicative of importance in a causal sense; Figure 4 is presented purely to provide insight into the structure of the fitted regression model.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement by the authors about interpretation of their results.

claim: A method for ranking variables in a causal framework applied to malaria case count data from Madagascar showed results very different from regression-based variable selection.
source: A method for ranking variables in a causal framework has recently been applied to the modelling of malaria case count data from health facilities in Madagascar and the results were shown to be very different to a regression-based variable selection method (Arambepola et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Arambepola et al., 2020.

claim: The spatially varying slope parameter fitted to each covariate may change sign in different parts of the country under the modelling framework.
source: Note also that the spatially varying slope parameter fitted to each covariate may even change sign in different parts of the country under our modelling framework.
evidence: This is a statement about the model structure and its flexibility.

claim: In Grand'Anse, a positive slope is assigned to elevation to penalize high elevations in the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range, while a negative slope is assigned to boost predicted incidence along the low-lying coastal fringe.
source: For instance, a positive slope is assigned to penalise high elevations in the Chaîne de la Selle mountain range of the Ouest and Sud-Est departments, while in Grand'Anse, a negative slope is assigned to boost the predicted incidence along the (low-lying) coastal fringe.
evidence: This is a description of how the model assigns different relationships in different regions.

claim: The catchment model allows patients in any location to split their attendance between multiple neighbouring facilities according to relative travel time and a relative attractiveness weight.
source: The structure of the catchment model used here (see the Materials and methods section for details) allows for patients in any given location to split their attendance between multiple neighbouring facilities according to the relative travel time to each (fixed input) and a relative attractiveness weight (free parameter learnt during fitting).
evidence: This is a description of the catchment model structure.

claim: The resulting catchments may have overlapping boundaries, which avoids unrealistic structural effects.
source: The resulting catchments may thus have overlapping boundaries, which avoids unrealistic structural effects – such as a systematic under-estimation of city health facility patient populations when commuters may otherwise be erroneously assigned to exclusively visit suburban facilities – but can be a challenge for visualisation.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages and challenges of the model structure.

claim: The dominant seasonal signal is a uniphasic seasonal profile evident across most of Haiti, with cases rising during October-November to a peak in December-January and declining rapidly from February to a low during April-May.
source: The dominant signal is a uniphasic seasonal profile evident across most of the country, and most notably the central valley, with cases rising during October–November to a peak in December–January and then declining rapidly from February to a low during April–May.
evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: A small number of locations, notably one hotspot on the northern coast of Grand'Anse near Jeremie, show a tentative suggestion of a biphasic character with a smaller second peak in June.
source: A small number of locations – notably one hotspot on the northern coast of Grand'Anse near the town of Jeremie – show a tentative suggestion of a biphasic character with a smaller, second peak in June.
evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis.

claim: The biphasic pattern near Jeremie may be an artefact of a recent epidemic outbreak that has not been entirely resolved by the cleaning and imputation procedure.
source: However, it is possible that this is an artefact of the recent epidemic outbreak in this area that has not been entirely resolved by our cleaning and imputation procedure for constructing a dataset of representative (endemic character) case counts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement by the authors about a potential limitation.

claim: In high incidence areas of the central valley and Grand'Anse, the most important positive covariate is the enhanced vegetation index lagged by 2 months.
source: In the high incidence areas of the central valley and the Grand'Anse, the most important positive covariate in a predictive sense is the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) lagged by 2 months
evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: In the central valley, the most important negative covariate is land surface temperature lagged by 1 month.
source: while the most important negative covariate is the land surface temperature (LST) lagged by 1 month in the former
evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: In Grand'Anse, the most important negative covariate is the enhanced vegetation index unlagged.
source: and the EVI unlagged in the latter
evidence: This is a finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis, as illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The fitted model covariates should not be directly interpreted as physical drivers of malaria incidence because the model is designed from a predictive framework rather than one of causal inference.
source: Again, note that although these covariates may plausibly reflect physical drivers of malaria incidence in Haiti, we caution against this direct interpretation as the fitted model is designed from a predictive framework rather than one of causal inference.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement by the authors about interpretation.

claim: All climatic and vegetation cover covariates are highly co-linear.
source: Moreover, all of these climatic and vegetation cover covariates are themselves highly co-linear, so upon exclusion of one there is typically another able to be identified as providing an explanatory contribution of similar magnitude within the regression model.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical properties of the covariates.

claim: The TAS program used serological markers of long-term malaria exposure (AMA and MSP antigenic responses) to characterize malaria endemicity in school-aged children.
source: The TAS program used serological markers of long-term malaria exposure – apical membrane antigen (AMA) and merozoite surface protein (MSP) antigenic responses – to characterise malaria endemicity in school-aged children.
evidence: This is a description of the TAS program methodology.

claim: The median-to-median correlation between TAS sero-prevalence and predicted clinical incidence rate has a Pearson coefficient of 0.426 (95% CI: 0.353–0.499).
source: The median-to-median correlation between these two metrics of transmission intensity has a Pearson coefficient of 0.426 (95% CI: 0.353–0.499), reflecting a positive but noisy relationship.
evidence: This is a quantitative validation result from comparing model predictions to TAS data.

claim: Much of the width in the scatter plot between TAS sero-prevalence and predicted incidence derives from random sampling noise.
source: Of course, since the TAS sample size per school is generally small (<30), the credible intervals around these point estimates of sero-prevalence are correspondingly broad. When considered in addition to the uncertainties surrounding the fine-scale predictions from our health facility-based model, it is likely that much of the width in this scatter plot derives from random (sampling) noise.
evidence: This is an inference about the sources of uncertainty in the validation comparison.

claim: There is a discrepancy between moderate to high sero-prevalence schools in the Nord department and low predicted clinical incidence rate from the health facility dataset.
source: Where visual comparison of Figure 8A to Figure 1A indicates the most interesting discrepancy is with regard to the presence of some moderate (and in one case, high) sero-prevalence schools in the Nord department for which our predicted clinical incidence rate from the health facility dataset is everywhere rather low.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing Figure 8A to Figure 1A.

claim: The discrepancy in Nord department is suspected to reflect a strong decline in transmission intensity over the period 2014-2016.
source: We suspect that this is a reflection of a strong decline in transmission intensity in this region over the period 2014–2016, seen in the rapid decline in cases reported and hence the strong de-trending in our model towards the 2019 case counts
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation by the authors.

claim: It is not possible to unambiguously distinguish changes to the health reporting system from genuine transmission intensity trends from the available data.
source: although it is not possible to unambiguously distinguish changes to the health reporting system from genuine transmission intensity trends from the available data.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the data.

claim: The incidence surfaces should be understood as reflecting the current state of transmission subject to recent history of anti-malarial interventions, rather than inherent environmental receptivity under a zero intervention scenario.
source: An important point raised by this comparison is that the incidence surfaces presented here should be understood as reflecting the current state of transmission subject to the recent history of anti-malarial interventions, rather than as a reflection of the inherent environmental receptivity under a zero intervention scenario.
evidence: This is an important interpretive caveat provided by the authors.

claim: A minimal alternative approach using naïve imputation and naïve catchment structure yields a correlation coefficient of 0.301 (95% CI: 0.215–0.369) against TAS sero-prevalence data.
source: The correlation coefficient of this risk map against the TAS sero-prevalence data is just 0.301 (95% CI: 0.215–0.369), compared against 0.426 (95% CI: 0.353–0.499) for our preferred model.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison showing the preferred model performs better.

claim: Using de-trending, imputing, and diagnostic correcting on the naïve catchment model improves the correlation against TAS sero-prevalences to 0.331 (95% CI: 0.257–0.398).
source: A second version of the naïve catchment risk map is shown in Figure 9B, this time after using our Step one and Step two models (see Materials and methods) for de-trending, imputing, and diagnostic correcting the raw case data. Overall, this adjustment improves the correlation against the TAS sero-prevalences to 0.331 (95% CI: 0.257–0.398).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison showing the value of the data processing steps.

claim: The naïve approach would suggest that transmission in Grand'Anse is dominated by hotspots sharply concentrated on the townships of Abricots, Bonbon, Anse-d'Hainault, and Les Irois with transmission intensity above 100 cases per 1000 PYO in each.
source: Compared with our preferred model-based risk map (Figure 1), the result here would suggest that transmission in the Grand'Anse is dominated by hotspots sharply concentrated on the townships of Abricots, Bonbon, Anse-d'Hainault, and Les Irois, with transmission intensity above 100 cases per 1000 PYO in each, rather than being spread more evenly throughout the coastal settlements and rural communities of this peninsula.
evidence: This is a comparison of the naïve approach results to the preferred model.

claim: The fine-scale mapping brings a greatly refined understanding of the elimination challenge in Haiti.
source: The fine-scale mapping of malaria incidence and its seasonality profile in Haiti achieved through our fitting of a Bayesian geospatial regression framework with catchment sub-model to the 2014–2019 health facility case reports brings a greatly refined understanding of the elimination challenge on this side of Hispaniola.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the value of the study.

claim: Communities suffering from the highest annual average rates of clinical malaria (above 50 cases per 1000 PYO) in 2019 are those along the coastline and valleys of the Grand'Anse and Sud departments.
source: We see that the communities suffering from the highest annual average rates of clinical malaria (above 50 cases per 1000 PYO) in 2019 are those along the coastline and valleys of the Grand'Anse and Sud departments.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the model analysis.

claim: Additional pockets of low-to-moderate endemicity (1-10 cases per 1000 PYO) are located in the central valley spanning Artibonite and Centre departments, in some coastal communities of Nippes, Sud-Est, and Nord-Est departments, and surrounding Port-au-Prince in Ouest department.
source: Additional pockets of low-to-moderate endemicity (1–10 cases per 1000 PYO) are located in the central valley spanning the Artibonite and Centre departments, in some coastal communities of the Nippes, Sud-Est, and Nord-Est departments, and surrounding Port-au-Prince in the Ouest department
evidence: This is a summary finding from the model analysis.

claim: The area surrounding Port-au-Prince accounts for a substantial proportion of total cases each year owing to the size of the population.
source: the latter accounting for a substantial proportion of the total cases each year owing to the size of the population in this area.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of incidence rates and population density.

claim: The Nord and Nord-Est departments have lower incidence rates (below 1 case per 1000 PYO), and some areas can be confidently predicted as extremely low (below 1 case per 10,000 PYO).
source: The Nord and Nord-Est departments have lower incidence rates (below 1 case per 1000 PYO), and some areas can yet be confidently predicted as extremely low (below 1 case per 10,000 PYO).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the model analysis.

claim: There exists substantial heterogeneity in the clinical incidence rate of malaria at small scales within departments.
source: Against these broad variations between departments, there exists substantial heterogeneity in the clinical incidence rate of malaria at rather small scales within departments
evidence: This is a summary finding from the model analysis.

claim: In a predictive sense, heterogeneity within departments can be explained by differences in accessibility, elevation, road presence/absence, and potential evapotranspiration.
source: which in a predictive sense can be explained within our modelling approach by differences in accessibility, elevation, road presence/absence, and potential evapotranspiration.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's covariate findings.

claim: The clinical incidence of malaria in Haiti is highly seasonal with a strong uniphasic seasonality pattern at maximum during December-January and minimum during April-May.
source: The clinical incidence of malaria in Haiti is also highly seasonal with a strong uniphasic seasonality pattern at maximum during December–January and minimum during April–May.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the spatio-temporal model analysis.

claim: The maps have been used to derive epidemiologically relevant operational units for targeting packages of interventions in five priority communes in Grand'Anse.
source: These maps have been used to derive epidemiologically relevant operational units for targeting packages of interventions in five priority communes in Grand'Anse.
evidence: This is a statement about the application of the study outputs.

claim: Operational units were ranked by the strength of transmission (quantified in terms of the reproduction number under control, Rc) to help determine those that would receive targeted mass drug administration and IRS in 2018.
source: Operational units were ranked by the strength of transmission (quantified after further post-processing in terms of the reproduction number under control, Rc) to help determine those that would receive targeted mass drug administration (tMDA) and with IRS in 2018, and are again being used in planning this year (2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the application of the study outputs.

claim: Serological data were subsequently used to refine the ordering of operational units.
source: Serological data were subsequently used to refine this ordering, and an eventual re-definition of operational unit boundaries was made to follow natural logistical divisions such as rivers and major roads.
evidence: This is a statement about how additional data were used in planning.

claim: Fine-scale probabilistic maps offer a more nuanced stratification than categorical risk maps at the commune level produced by direct summary of case counts divided by areal population totals.
source: For planning purposes such as these, it is clear that these fine-scale probabilistic maps offer a more nuanced stratification than the categorical risk maps at the commune level produced, e.g., for the World Malaria Report (World Health Organization, 2019), by direct summary of the available case counts divided by areal population totals
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the value of the approach, with citation to World Health Organization, 2019.

claim: Fine-scale probabilistic maps are far superior to dichotomous risk maps based solely on elevation at a threshold of 500 m that have been used in past decision making.
source: and one that is far superior to the dichotomous risk maps based solely on elevation (at a threshold of 500 m) that have, anecdotally, been used in past decision making.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the value of the approach.

claim: There is a lack of information regarding potential spatial variations in treatment seeking behaviour across Haiti.
source: Of particular concern is the lack of information regarding potential spatial variations in treatment seeking behaviour across the country.
evidence: This is a statement about a data limitation.

claim: A recent study confirmed that some Haitians will seek care for febrile illness outside the national health care system, such as at a traditional healer or at a private health care provider not reporting to the national network.
source: A recent study of community attitudes towards malaria treatment (Druetz et al., 2018) confirmed that some Haitians will seek care for febrile illness outside the national health care system, such as at a traditional healer or at a private health care provider not reporting to the national network.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Druetz et al., 2018.

claim: The study attempted to adjust for the possible effect of travel-time distance on absolute treatment seeking propensity using a model calibrated to an African setting.
source: At present, we have attempted only to adjust for the possible effect of travel-time distance on the absolute treatment seeking propensity, using a model calibrated to an African setting (Alegana et al., 2012); clearly, this deserves refinement if local data can be gathered through a dedicated survey questionnaire.
evidence: This is a statement about the model approach and its limitations, with citation to Alegana et al., 2012.

claim: Seasonal migrations of agricultural workers or other large itinerant groups have potential to introduce spurious effects into modelled case incidence rates unless explicitly accounted for via a dynamic population denominator.
source: It is known that seasonal migrations of agricultural workers or other large itinerant groups have a potential to introduce spurious effects into modelled case incidence rates unless explicitly accounted for via a dynamic population denominator (Zu Erbach-Schoenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zu Erbach-Schoenberg et al., 2016.

claim: High-fidelity human movement data is not currently available for Haiti.
source: As high-fidelity human movement data is not currently available for Haiti, we cannot yet model this aspect directly and can only hope that a substantial proportion of any such unmodelled variation is absorbed implicitly within the random effects terms of our statistical model.
evidence: This is a statement about a data limitation.

claim: An earlier study indicated that the Ouest department containing Port-au-Prince is more strongly connected to all other departments than any of those departments are connected with each other independently.
source: Interestingly, an earlier study in which a regression model was built to predict short-term human movement from internal migration data (Sorichetta et al., 2016) has indicated that in relative terms the Ouest department containing Port-au-Prince is more strongly connected to all other departments than any of those departments are connected with each other independently, although the magnitude of this connectivity in absolute terms remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sorichetta et al., 2016.

claim: The model aims only to map where people at risk of malaria illness reside, which may not necessarily be the same as where they contracted their infection.
source: It is worth emphasising here that our model aims only to map where people at risk of malaria illness reside, which may not necessarily be the same as where they contracted their infection.
evidence: This is a clarification about what the model does and does not capture.

claim: The higher risk communities identified in the modelling are primarily in remote and rural areas where people are unlikely to regularly commute long distances.
source: The higher risk communities identified in our modelling are primarily in remote and rural areas, in which people are unlikely to regularly commute long distances from their place of residence for work or leisure.
evidence: This is an inference about the characteristics of high-risk areas.

claim: There are a substantial number of people in the vicinity of Port-au-Prince presenting to health facilities with clinical malaria.
source: However, in terms of absolute case numbers it was shown in Figure 1B that there are a substantial number of people in the vicinity of Port-au-Prince presenting to health facilities with clinical malaria.
evidence: This is a finding from Figure 1B.

claim: Whether infections in Port-au-Prince were contracted locally or elsewhere, and what role seasonal migration and/or travel plays in sustaining transmission, is not informed by the present dataset.
source: Whether these infections were contracted locally or elsewhere – and what role seasonal migration and/or travel plays in sustaining transmission wherever it occurs – is not informed by the present dataset.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the data.

claim: The introduction of a gravity-style representation with overlapping catchments based on travel-time distances constitutes a substantial effort towards constructing a realistic representation of patient behaviours.
source: Our introduction of a gravity-style representation with overlapping catchments based on travel-time distances constitutes a substantial effort towards constructing a realistic representation of patient behaviours, especially in comparison with the vanilla alternatives of Euclidean ('as-the-crow-flies') distances and/or hard (tessellation-style) boundaries
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The catchment model is still a profound simplification despite being more sophisticated than vanilla alternatives.
source: yet there is no doubt that our model is still a profound simplification.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of model limitations.

claim: Comparison against TAS serological data suggests the model is on the right track for accurately downscaling health facility data to pixel level.
source: It remains for future research to establish how much of a limitation this is in terms of our ability to accurately downscale health facility data to pixel level – though at least our comparison against the TAS serological data suggests we are on the right track
evidence: This is an inference based on the validation results.

claim: Work has begun to explore risk mapping under more complex catchment sub-models in a focus region of the Artibonite department where partial case tracing has been performed.
source: Already we have begun work (van den Hoogen et al., in prep.) to explore risk mapping under more complex catchment sub-models in a focus region of the Artibonite department where partial case tracing of febrile patients (from health facility to patient household location) has been performed.
evidence: This is a statement about ongoing research.

claim: Catchments reconstructed in the Artibonite case tracing study confirm a general dependence on travel time but also reveal instances where clusters of patients travel far beyond their nearest facility to seek care.
source: The catchments we have begun to reconstruct in the Artibonite case tracing study do confirm a general dependence on travel time, but they also reveal instances in which clusters of patients travel far beyond their nearest facility to seek care.
evidence: This is a finding from ongoing work in the Artibonite region.

claim: Lower income patients may be avoiding facilities that illegally charge for anti-malarial medication.
source: We do not have data on specific factors, which might help to explain this behaviour, though anecdotal examples that appear in the literature suggest possible explanations, e.g., lower income patients may be avoiding a facility that illegally charges for anti-malarial medication (Druetz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Druetz et al., 2018.

claim: The authors are exploring inclusion of information from alternative malaria metrics such as sero-positivity rate to further refine risk maps.
source: Another direction we are exploring to further refine our risk maps is the inclusion of information from alternative malaria metrics such as the sero-positvity rate, used here only for model validation.
evidence: This is a statement about ongoing research directions.

claim: The same principles of model-based geostatistics can be applied to refine sero-prevalence estimates via spatial covariates and spatially correlated noise models.
source: Important to note is that, although our current validation model treats the underlying sero-prevalence at each site as an independent random variable, one can readily apply the same principles of model-based geostatistics to refine sero-prevalence estimates via spatial covariates and spatially correlated noise models (Ashton et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ashton et al., 2015.

claim: Developing appropriate methods for simultaneous modelling of multiple data types is an active topic of research within geospatial statistics.
source: More challenging is to develop appropriate methods for the simultaneous modelling of multiple data types. Indeed this is an active topic of research within geospatial statistics – both in regard to linking point data with areal data (Richardson and Best, 2003; Moraga et al., 2017) and in regard to sharing information between multiple disease metrics (for the same disease or even different diseases [Held et al., 2005])
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Richardson and Best, 2003; Moraga et al., 2017; and Held et al., 2005.

claim: The authors are pursuing simultaneous modelling of multiple data types for further refinement of incidence maps in the Grand'Anse department.
source: and is a direction we are pursuing for further refinement of our incidence maps in the Grand'Anse department (Amratia et al., in prep.).
evidence: This is a statement about ongoing research.

claim: Point of care case counts can be used to generate programmatically useful maps of clinical incidence rates providing fine-scale risk stratifications.
source: In conclusion, the analyses and results of this paper demonstrate that point of care case counts can be used to generate programmatically useful maps of clinical incidence rates providing fine-scale risk stratifications.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: A spatio-temporal seasonality profile can be determined when data are available at monthly intervals.
source: A spatio-temporal seasonality profile can also be determined when data are available at monthly intervals.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: The information from these maps can be used to refine the spatial and/or temporal targeting of high-burden areas for anti-malarial interventions such as tMDA, IRS, and long-lasting insecticidal net delivery.
source: This information can be used to refine the spatial and/or temporal targeting of high-burden areas for anti-malarial interventions such as tMDA, IRS, and long-lasting insecticidal net delivery.
evidence: This is a statement about the application value of the study outputs.

claim: The outputs are readily updatable as additional facility data are made available.
source: These outputs are readily updatable as additional facility data are made available
evidence: This is a statement about the sustainability of the approach.

claim: The outputs will be valuable in defining residual transmission foci as the final stages of elimination near.
source: and will be valuable in defining residual transmission foci as the final stages of elimination near.
evidence: This is a statement about the future value of the approach.

claim: The primary dataset consisted of monthly counts of confirmed malaria cases for 771 geo-located health facilities reporting at least once in 2019.
source: Our primary dataset consisted of monthly counts of confirmed malaria cases – i.e., patients seeking care for febrile illness with patent parasitaemia detected via RDT or microscopy – for each of 771 geo-located health facilities reporting at least once in 2019.
evidence: This is a description of the primary data source.

claim: The 771 facilities are a sub-set of 1191 facilities in a master reporting file compiled by the PNCM of Haiti with assistance from CHAI.
source: These 771 facilities are a sub-set of the 1191 facilities in a master reporting file compiled by the PNCM of Haiti with assistance from the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI)
evidence: This is a description of the data source.

claim: Since 2016, CHWs attached to certain health facilities have been proactively seeking cases in the local community, and these cases were added to the reported totals.
source: Since 2016, CHWs attached to certain health facilities have been proactively seeking cases in the local community, and we add these cases to the reported totals of ordinary patient visits for those facilities.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing.

claim: The reporting period covered by the dataset begins with January 2014 and finishes with December 2019.
source: The reporting period covered by this dataset begins with January 2014 and finishes with December 2019
evidence: This is a description of the temporal extent of the data.

claim: The overall completeness of reporting among the 771 facilities is 77.5%.
source: and the overall completeness of reporting among the sub-set of 771 facilities is 77.5%
evidence: This is a quantitative description of data completeness.

claim: 537 facilities reported in at least 61 of the 72 months (69.6%).
source: with 537 facilities reporting in at least 61 of the 72 months (69.6%).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of data completeness.

claim: After imputing missing monthly case reports and aggregating nearly co-located facilities using hierarchical clustering, a total of 450 'aggregate pseudo-facilities' were formed.
source: After imputing missing monthly case reports for all 771 facilities reporting in 2019 (as described in stage one of our inference procedure below), we reduce the subsequent model complexity by aggregating nearly co-located facilities using a hierarchical clustering algorithm. In this way, a total of 450 'aggregate pseudo-facilities' are formed which we will simply continue to refer to as 'health facilities'.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing procedure.

claim: A suite of high-resolution satellite imaging products were introduced as covariates within the statistical modelling.
source: A suite of high-resolution satellite imaging products were introduced as covariates within our statistical modelling.
evidence: This is a description of the model inputs.

claim: The High Resolution Settlement Layer from Facebook provides the population denominator for the model.
source: The High Resolution Settlement Layer from the Connectivity Lab at Facebook (URL: https://www.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/hrsl/) provides the population denominator for our model
evidence: This is a description of a key data input.

claim: The Weiss et al., 2018 friction surface is used to build travel-time maps from each 1×1 km pixel to each health facility.
source: and the Weiss et al., 2018 friction surface is used to build travel-time maps from each 1 × 1 km pixel to each health facility with assistance from the malariaAtlas R package (Pfeffer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of a key data input, with citations to Weiss et al., 2018 and Pfeffer et al., 2018.

claim: Serological prevalence observations for 24,514 children aged 6 and 7 years old in 820 schools from the Integrated TAS datasets sampled between November 2014 and August 2016 were used for validation.
source: Serological prevalence observations (AMA and MSP antigens) for 24,514 children aged 6 and 7 years old in 820 schools from the Integrated TAD datasets (Knipes et al., 2017) sampled from across Haiti between November 2014 and August 2016 were used for validation of the spatial trends revealed in the annual incidence outputs.
evidence: This is a description of the validation data, with citation to Knipes et al., 2017.

claim: The stepwise inference framework is designed to limit the impact of confounding factors on model-based estimates while negotiating a trade-off between theoretical advantages of explicit representation and computational advantages of model parsimony.
source: The stepwise inference framework described below is designed to limit the impact of such factors on our model-based estimates while negotiating a pragmatic trade-off between the theoretical advantages of building an explicit representation of each conceivable error term and the computational advantages of model parsimony.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach and its rationale.

claim: Inference of fine-scale case incidence rate and seasonality profile is modularised in three distinct stages.
source: Our inference of the fine-scale case incidence rate and seasonality profile of clinical malaria in Haiti is thus modularised in three distinct stages.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological structure.

claim: In the first stage, statistical models are used to impute missing data and de-trend reported monthly case counts from 2014 to 2019 towards an RDT-standardised 2019 level.
source: In the first stage, a pair of statistical models is used to impute missing data and de-trend the reported monthly case counts from 2014 to 2019 at each facility towards an RDT-standardised 2019 level.
evidence: This is a description of the first stage of the methodology.

claim: In the second stage, a fine-scale spatial-only geostatistical model with flexible catchment sub-model is fit to estimate annual average incidence rate at pixel-level and attractiveness of each health facility.
source: In the second stage, a fine-scale, spatial-only geostatistical model with a flexible catchment sub-model is fit to (each modular posterior draw of) the representative dataset to estimate the annual average incidence rate at pixel-level and the attractiveness of each health facility.
evidence: This is a description of the second stage of the methodology.

claim: In the third stage, a fine-scale spatio-temporal geostatistical model is fit conditional on the previously fitted catchment sub-model to explain residual seasonal variation.
source: In the third and final stage, a fine-scale spatio-temporal geostatistical model is fit (conditional on the previously fitted catchment sub-model) to explain the residual seasonal variation about (each modular posterior sample of) this baseline risk surface in the (corresponding sample of) representative monthly case data.
evidence: This is a description of the third stage of the methodology.

claim: Modularisation can guard against magnification of systematic errors between components due to misspecification in one of them.
source: Although the primary motivation for introducing these 'cuts' (Plummer, 2015) in our inferential approach is, as noted above, to focus on endemic transmission, promote model parsimony, and improve computational feasibility in model fitting, it is worth noting that such contained modularisation can also guard against the magnification of systematic errors between components due to a misspecification in one of them (Jacob, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological advantages, with citations to Plummer, 2015 and Jacob, 2017.

claim: Almost 96.4% of pixels with non-zero population density lie within 100 minutes travel time from their nearest health facility.
source: However, very little decline is seen until beyond 100 min travel time in well-studied settings (such as Namibia [Alegana et al., 2012]), and at the 1 × 1 km resolution of our map making almost 96.4% of pixels with non-zero population density lies within this distance from their nearest health facility.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about accessibility in Haiti, with citation to Alegana et al., 2012.

claim: A novel hierarchical Bayesian modelling framework was developed in which a latent pixel-level incidence surface with spatio-temporal innovations is linked to observed case data via a flexible catchment sub-model.
source: To this end, a novel hierarchical Bayesian modelling framework was developed in which a latent, pixel-level incidence surface with spatio-temporal innovations is linked to the observed case data via a flexible catchment sub-model designed to account for the absence of data on case household locations.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological contribution from the abstract.

claim: The model was fitted using monthly case counts from 771 health facilities reporting from across Haiti throughout the 6-year period from January 2014 to December 2019.
source: Here we present a key piece of this planning: an up-to-date, fine-scale endemicity map and seasonality profile for Haiti informed by monthly case counts from 771 health facilities reporting from across the country throughout the 6-year period from January 2014 to December 2019.
evidence: This is a description of the data used from the abstract.
